topicTitle: How Code Executes: Call Stack & Execution Context

lessons.title: Creation Phase vs Execution Phase in JavaScript Engines
lessons.description: JavaScript doesn't just run code line by line — it first scans for declarations before executing anything.

sections.heading: Two distinct phases
paragraphs: When JavaScript runs your code, it goes through two phases before any code actually executes. Understanding this explains why some things work even before they're defined.
list: Creation phase — the engine scans for declarations (variables, functions) and sets up memory
Execution phase — the engine runs the code line by line
Functions are fully stored during creation — variables get undefined
This is why you can call a function before its declaration but not read a variable

codeExamples.heading: Function hoisting in action
explanation: During creation, the engine stores the function body — so it's available before the line.
Variables declared with let/const are created but not initialized — reading them throws an error.
This two-phase behavior is the engine's way of preparing memory before running code.

practice.task: Write code that calls a function before it's declared. Then try the same with a variable declared with let and observe the different behavior.
hints: Define a function declaration and call it above the definition.
Define a let variable and try to log it above the declaration.
Note the function works but the variable throws an error.

keyTakeaways: JavaScript has a creation phase (memory setup) and an execution phase (line-by-line running).
Function declarations are fully hoisted — you can call them before they appear in the code.
Variables with let/const are in the Temporal Dead Zone during creation — reading them early throws an error.
Understanding these phases explains seemingly strange JavaScript behavior.
lessons.challenge: Explain why typeof works on undeclared variables but console.log doesn't.

lessons.title: Global Execution Context vs Function Execution Context
lessons.description: Every piece of JavaScript runs inside an execution context — global or function.

sections.heading: What is an execution context?
paragraphs: An execution context is like a box that holds everything needed to run a piece of code: the variables, the scope, and the this value. There are three types.
list: Global execution context — created when the script starts; one per program
Function execution context — created each time a function is called
Eval execution context — created inside eval() (avoid using eval)
Each context has its own variable environment and scope chain

codeExamples.heading: How contexts are created
explanation: The global context runs first — creating globalVar and the functions.
Calling outer() creates a new execution context for that function.
Calling inner() inside outer creates a third context.
When each function returns, its context is destroyed and its local variables are freed.

practice.task: Write a nested function structure with 3 levels. Log a variable from each level inside the innermost function to see how context nesting works.
hints: Create global, outer and inner functions with variables at each level.
Call the inner function from outer, and outer from global.
Inside inner, log variables from all three levels.

keyTakeaways: The global execution context is created once when the script starts.
A new function execution context is created every time a function is called.
Inner functions can access variables from outer contexts (scope chain).
Execution contexts are destroyed when the function finishes executing.
lessons.challenge: Trace the execution context creation order for a program with a global variable, a function call, and a nested function call.

lessons.title: Stack Frames & Call Stack Execution Tracing
lessons.description: JavaScript uses a call stack to track which function is currently running and in what order.

sections.heading: The call stack
paragraphs: The call stack is a data structure that tracks function calls. Each time a function is called, a new frame is pushed on top. When it returns, the frame is popped off.
list: Stacks are LIFO — Last In, First Out
The function on top is the one currently executing
When a function calls another, a new frame is added on top
When a function returns, its frame is removed

codeExamples.heading: Tracing the call stack
explanation: first() is pushed onto the stack and starts executing.
It calls second() — pushed on top of first.
When third() returns, it's popped. Then second returns, then first.

practice.task: Create three functions where A calls B and B calls C. Log a message at the start and end of each function. Predict and verify the output order.
hints: Log "A start" then call B, then log "A end".
Do the same for B calling C.
The output should nest: A start → B start → C → B end → A end.

keyTakeaways: The call stack tracks function execution using LIFO order (Last In, First Out).
Each function call pushes a new frame onto the stack.
When a function returns, its frame is popped and execution resumes in the caller.
The output of nested function calls reveals the stack's LIFO behavior.
lessons.challenge: Use console.trace() inside a deeply nested function to see the actual call stack printed in the console.

lessons.title: Stack Overflow Errors & Recursion Limits
lessons.description: Infinite or deep recursion fills the call stack until it overflows — understand how to avoid it.

sections.heading: What causes a stack overflow?
paragraphs: Every call stack has a fixed size. If a function keeps calling itself without stopping, the stack grows until it exceeds the limit and throws a RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.
list: Infinite recursion: a function that calls itself without a base case
Deep recursion: a function calling itself thousands of times
The limit varies by browser but is usually around 10,000–25,000 frames
Stack overflow crashes the current script execution

codeExamples.heading: Stack overflow and base cases
explanation: The first function never stops calling itself — the stack grows infinitely.
The second function checks n <= 0 before recursing — this is the base case.
Every recursive function needs a base case to prevent stack overflow.
Think of it as: "When should I stop?" — that's your base case.

practice.task: Write a recursive function that calculates factorial (n!). Include a base case for n = 0 or n = 1. Test with n = 5 and n = 10.

keyTakeaways: The call stack has a fixed size — infinite recursion causes a stack overflow.
Every recursive function needs a base case to stop calling itself.
Stack overflow throws a RangeError and crashes the current script.
When debugging recursion, always verify the base case is reachable.
lessons.challenge: Write a recursive function that flattens a nested array. Include a base case for non-array elements and test with arrays nested 3+ levels deep.
